chief_complaint: sudden sharp flank pain radiating to groin with hematuria
hpi_details: A 56-year-old female presents to the clinic with sudden sharp flank pain radiating to groin with hematuria. The patient states the symptoms started recently and have been gradually worsening, accompanied by generalized fatigue.
ideas: thinks it might be a kidney stone, since her father has had them before
concerns: She is worried the blood in her urine could be cancer like her older sister had.
expectations: She hopes to receive a strong painkiller right away so she can get through the day without agony.

investigation_events.title: Urgent ureteric colic investigations
investigation_events.availability_message: Urinalysis and non-contrast CT KUB results are now available. Analgesia should not be delayed while obtaining imaging.

results.value: 3+ blood with numerous RBCs; no pyuria or nitrites
6 mm left distal ureteral calculus with mild upstream hydronephrosis

core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Nephrolithiasis (Kidney Stone) is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Standard management emphasizes analgesia, adequate hydration, and selective use of alpha-blocker therapy (tamsulosin) for an appropriately sized distal ureteral stone to aid passage, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: sudden sharp flank pain radiating to groin with hematuria

Key HPI features: A 56-year-old female presents to the clinic with sudden sharp flank pain radiating to groin with hematuria. The patient states the symptoms started recently and have been gradually worsening, accompanied by generalized fatigue.

Objective/Exam findings: Vitals: BP 138/86, HR 96, afebrile; patient restless and unable to find a comfortable position. Left costovertebral angle tenderness; abdomen soft without rebound or guarding. Labs: Urinalysis with microscopic/gross hematuria, no pyuria or nitrites. Non-contrast CT KUB: 6mm left distal ureteral stone with mild hydronephrosis. Basic metabolic panel and white count normal.
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Nephrolithiasis (Kidney Stone).
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Pyelonephritis without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Fever with flank pain — suggests an infected obstructing stone, a urologic emergency.
management_principles: Assess for infection, solitary kidney, or renal impairment that would require urgent urologic evaluation
Provide NSAID analgesia (e.g., ketorolac) when safe, encourage adequate hydration, and consider tamsulosin for an appropriately sized distal ureteral stone to aid passage
Strain urine for stone analysis, arrange follow-up imaging, and counsel on dietary/fluid modification to reduce recurrence
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

source_refs.title: KDIGO 2024 Clinical Practice Guideline for Kidney Disease

reference_soap.subjective:
Chief Complaint: sudden sharp flank pain radiating to groin with hematuria

A 56-year-old female presents with sudden-onset severe left flank pain radiating to the groin, associated with visible blood in the urine and nausea. Reports restlessness and being unable to find a comfortable position. Denies fever or chills.
reference_soap.objective: Vitals: BP 138/86, HR 96, afebrile; patient restless and unable to find a comfortable position. Left costovertebral angle tenderness; abdomen soft without rebound or guarding. Labs: Urinalysis with microscopic/gross hematuria, no pyuria or nitrites. Non-contrast CT KUB: 6mm left distal ureteral stone with mild hydronephrosis. Basic metabolic panel and white count normal.
reference_soap.assessment: Acute nephrolithiasis (likely calcium oxalate stone) causing left ureteral colic, with an obstructing 6mm distal ureteral stone on CT and no evidence of infection.
reference_soap.plan: Assess for infection, solitary kidney, renal impairment, and uncontrolled symptoms, which require urgent urologic evaluation. Provide NSAID analgesia when safe and encourage normal hydration. Consider tamsulosin selectively for an appropriate distal ureteral stone rather than routinely; strain recovered stones for analysis and arrange imaging/follow-up.

learning_objectives: Recognize clinical presentation and diagnostic markers of Nephrolithiasis
Select appropriate diagnostic workup for Nephrolithiasis
Implement evidence-based management plan: Hydration, NSAIDs, Tamsulosin, strain urine for stone analysis

teaching.one_liner: A calcium oxalate or uric acid stone forms in the kidney and becomes lodged in the ureter, causing sudden severe colicky flank pain radiating to the groin with visible blood in the urine.
red_flags: Fever with flank pain — suggests an infected obstructing stone, a urologic emergency

must_ask.say: Where did the pain start, and does it move to your groin?
How suddenly did the pain start?
Have you noticed blood in your urine?
Have you had kidney stones before?

history.answer: Doctor, I suddenly got this excruciating sharp pain in my left flank earlier today, and when I went to the bathroom, my urine was visibly pink and bloody.
The pain hit me completely out of the blue about four hours ago while I was at my desk, and it quickly became intense.
It started deep in my left side and back, and then it began traveling down toward my lower belly and left groin.
Yes, it radiates down from my left flank directly into my left groin and lower abdomen.
It is an intense, sharp, stabbing pain that comes in severe waves, making it impossible to sit still.
It is an eight or nine out of ten. It keeps pulsing and cramping in waves of severe intensity.
Nothing makes it better, no matter how I sit or lie down. Moving around does not help either, but I just cannot stay still.
No, I have never experienced pain like this in my life.
I have felt really nauseated since the pain started, but I have not actually thrown up.
My bowels have been normal, with no diarrhea, constipation, or blood in my stool. I can still pass gas normally.
No, I have not had any fever or chills.
No, my skin and eyes look normal to me, and my stool has its usual brown color.
I noticed red, pinkish blood in my urine when I went earlier. It hurts slightly when I urinate, and I feel like I need to go more often.
No, I have not felt faint, lightheaded, or dizzy at all.
No, there is definitely no vaginal bleeding or unusual vaginal discharge.
No chest pain, palpitations, or trouble catching my breath.
history.topic: Chest pain and shortness of breath

history.answer: I just had a light salad with grilled chicken for lunch, nothing greasy or unusual, and I have not had any alcohol today.
I took two ibuprofen tablets about an hour ago when the pain became unbearable, but they did not help at all.
No, I have never had heart rhythm issues, blood clots, or vascular diseases.
I have never had kidney stones before, though my father used to suffer from them.
I am wondering if this could be a kidney stone, because my dad used to describe having pain just like this.
Seeing blood in my urine really terrified me because my sister passed away from cancer that started in her urinary tract.
I just desperately need something strong to take away this unbearable pain so I can stand up straight again.
I have always been healthy and have never been diagnosed with any chronic medical conditions.
I have never had any surgeries or been admitted to the hospital.
I do not take any prescription medications or regular daily supplements.
I have no known allergies to any medications or foods.
I have never smoked cigarettes.
I only have an occasional glass of wine on weekends with dinner, maybe once or twice a month.
I work as an office accountant and live with my husband. My job is mostly sedentary.
My father had recurring kidney stones, but there is no family history of kidney failure, cancer, or heart problems.
I went through menopause five years ago and have not had a period since, so there is no possibility of pregnancy.

exam.finding: The patient appears distressed, visibly uncomfortable, and is continuously shifting and pacing to find a comfortable position.
Blood pressure is 138/86 mmHg, pulse 96 beats per minute, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius, and oxygen saturation 99% on ambient air.
Abdomen is flat with no surgical scars, distension, visible peristalsis, or skin discoloration.
Normal bowel sounds are present across all four quadrants with no vascular bruits.
Abdomen is soft with no palpable masses or localized tenderness on light and deep palpation.
No rebound tenderness or involuntary abdominal wall guarding is elicited.
Negative Murphy sign without inspiratory arrest during right upper quadrant palpation.
No tenderness at McBurney point; negative psoas and obturator signs.
Marked tenderness elicited on gentle percussion over the left costovertebral angle; no tenderness on the right side.
Normal external female genitalia with no cervical motion tenderness or adnexal mass.
